questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: For one, U of Guelph is the only university in Canada with an Animal Science program. Furthermore, the university in Guelph offered some very interesting courses. Other than that, I really wanted to try and live in Canada after being here on vacation several years ago.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy! I can definitely recommend registering in the university's START International program (it's free!) because you get to arrive earlier than the rest of the students, which means that you can settle in and get more used to everything before classes commence. Also, they provide a lot of useful information AND free food. :))

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The only assistance was the START International. You have to move all your luggage by yourself, and unless you know anyone in the country, you're pretty much on your own. People here are extremely friendly though, so you might be lucky to find someone to help you - or at least point you in the direction of help.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were a lot of options, and the housing portal was very easy to navigate. The only irritant was that we didn't know our housing assignments until the very last moment.. Thankfully, exchange students get prioritized for on-campus housing which is nice!

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: You can wish for residencies where the meal plans are optional and these mostly get assigned to exchange students. In these housings, you have a fully-equipped kitchen so you can cook all of your meals. The smallest meal plan is $300 CAD and I can definitely recommend purchasing it. It's so useful if you have a late day on campus and really don't want to go home and cook, or if you just want to buy lots of coffee. This meal plan worked perfectly for me!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
When I write "fully-equipped kitchen", it's important to note that the kitchen comes without ANY kinds of utensils, dishes, pots, pans or whatever you need. Luckily, you can buy all that stuff fairly cheaply at Walmart, Canadian Tire or a dollar store. I shared my residence with 2 others so we just split the cost of everything.
Also, the beds don't have any bedding, so you have to buy both a pillow, a comforter and sheets.

Living on campus - especially in West Residence - was perfect for me! It is a part of campus but it wasn't crowded or very noisy, and I personally loved that I had to walk past the horse paddocks every day.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: We didn't have to pay for laundry!

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The system itself was easy to navigate but one of the documents (for course registration) was stupidly tricky to fill out. It was a pdf but not one that you could edit. You either had to print it, fill it out by hand, and then scan it back onto your computer, or you had to purchase a subscription to Adobe to be able to fill out the boxes.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
There wasn't much to it.. If you just check your different email accounts regularly, they pretty much guide you through the process. The exchange coordinators at the host institution replied quickly, and the only problem I had with the process, was that I didn't know until late Spring if I was actually going..

The host institution only needed a few documents from me and after submitting them, I just had to wait until I got my acceptance letter. From there, I filled out my information and preferences in the housing portal and I started browsing on the university's home page.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Because I'm in Animal Science, I had a Science coordinator assigned to me and he helped me with all kinds of questions. If he didn't have the answer, he would help me figure out who to contact instead.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I had made a list of 10 courses and I got 5. Thankfully, I got the one courses that replaced a mandatory one from U of Copenhagen! I really liked all of my courses, so I was lucky. It also won't hurt emailing the professor in charge of a specific course, if you didn't get registered for it the first time around. They are more often than not willing to let you into the course anyway; you just have to fill out a waiver. And if you then end up having too many courses, you can always drop one (or two). You just have to do it before the last day of classes.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
See my comment above.

Also, if you have the chance, go for courses that you can't find in Denmark! I really enjoyed my Indigenous course!

I found that the level of education was generally lower than at home so don't sweat it if you end up with 5 courses. That being said, more 2nd and 3rd year courses tend to have midterms and exams so if you want to avoid that, try registering for 4th year courses.

All in all, take the time to look through the different programs and the courses they offer; you might find an interesting course that you didn't know existed.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: As I mentioned before, the academic level of education is generally lower than what we're used to in Europe, but most of my courses were still interesting.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
1. We weren't required to read anything before coming to the lectures. They had recommended readings but you didn't have to read it to be able to do well in the courses.

2. The lectures themselves were similar to those at UCPH, although we didn't really have guest speakers. Also, it seemed more like they were reading out loud from a script rather than making it engaging.

3. The assignments in most of my courses were graded by TA's (teacher's assistants) rather than the professors themselves. 

4. I only had 3-ish hours of lectures per course per week. Except for the one distant-education course, I was enrolled in. It took me between 30 and 60 minutes per week to finish the readings and the quizzes.

5. Assignments are much more important at my host university. On one hand, I really liked the fact that the grades from the assignments had an impact on the final grade. On the other hand, we had so many assignments that we just went from one to the other.. It got quite stressful sometimes.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
ANSC*4010 Animal Welfare Judging and Evaluation
ANSC*4560 Pet Nutrition
ENGL*1030 Effective writing
IES*1010 Intro to Indigenous Environmental Science and Practice

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would definitely recommend registering for an Indigenous course if you have the chance. It's a great way of learning about the different ways of thinking and acting, and it also gave me a better understanding of how Indigenous Peoples have been and still are being treated in today's society. Also, these courses tend to be more down to Earth, and we even had our lectures at the Arboretum at the north end of campus.

If you're in Animal Science and interested in nutrition, I would definitely choose Pet Nutrition as well. You'll get a better understanding of the different nutritional components of dog and cat food, and you'll even get to create your own recipe.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I ended up doing some traveling out west but other than that, I wasn't really surprised by any unexpected costs.
IMPORTANT! the housing fee had to paid in full before arrival! It wasn't paid on a monthly basis which means that I paid ~23000 DKK in August.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I think I was expecting things to be more expensive than at home but it turned out that groceries and books were around the same prices as in Denmark. Clothes etc. were a lot cheaper than at home!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: More than I could count! There were so many different things happening all the time that I didn't have time to go to even half of them.. There is definitely something for everyone - and I mean EVERYONE.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I found out that I really like going to hockey games - both the games at the university but also the ones in downtown Guelph.
In general, I will just recommend future exchange students to try as many different things as possible. Even if you don't find that one perfect club/activity, you will at least meet a lot of new, interesting people. It's a great way of making connections and maybe even friendships. 

TIP! Don't be afraid to go to an activity alone! People are more inclined to approach you if you're not surrounded by a bunch of people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Maybe rent a car and go hiking in the areas around Guelph. Or take a weekend trip to Toronto or Niagara Falls. On the weekend, the farmers' market in Guelph is open and it's just lovely! It's quite small but you can get some great things there. Their apple cider donuts are amazing!
There is a huge farmer's market in the neighboring city called St. Jacobs Farmers' Market and it's incredible. You could easily spend a whole day - or maybe even a full weekend - there!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
I found it very easy. Canadians are in general extremely friendly and helpful so if you just keep an open mind, you'll do just fine. 
One thing, that was tricky getting used to was mentally adding taxes to everything.. The price tags show the price without taxes so you have to mentally add the 13% yourself which takes some time getting used to. Especially at restaurants where you also have to tip the waiter.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: As mentioned before, don't be afraid to go to social gatherings alone and if you're just friendly and outgoing, it won't be difficult to socialize. Also, if you feel like you are bonding with someone, ask them to go out for a cup of coffee or to meet up for lunch on campus. I made some great friendships just by meeting up with a couple of people weekly.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The taxes.. ;))

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I absolutely loved the friendliness and openness I was met with most places! Although it didn't always seem sincere (especially in grocery stores), I really liked that people greet each other with "How are you?". Even if people couldn't care less about you or your day, it's still ingrained in them to be friendly. And then most of the time, people would actually mean it and it could just make my day being met with a smile and that question.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don't forget to enjoy your time in a different country! This is a once in a lifetime experience so make sure to not spend too much time studying. 

2. While enjoying the non-academic parts of the stay is essential, it's also important to keep up with your courses. It would be foolish to just make it go to waste by failing everything. Make an effort, please!

3. Make friends! Go to the different activities happening and see what happens. You are definitely going to become friends with some of the other exchange students but I can only recommend also getting to know some of the Canadian students.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: You will experience three seasons (Summer, Fall, Winter) while being there in the Fall semester so pack accordingly. Also, don't worry about packing Winter clothes; you can buy it when you get to Canada. This will also work out better for you since the clothes are more suited to the extreme weather changes compared to the things you get in DK. Especially boots and coats!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Just being there and experiencing a new country with everything that comes with it.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Knowing that the people, I got to know, are living so far away from me.. Some of the people, I met, became like family to me and I don't know when I'll get to see them again. :/

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: If you have a chance to go on exchange, GO! I cannot recommend it enough!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
